specAnchors.text: explain the trend in reactivity in Group 1 in terms of electronic configurations

primer.text: From Group 1 (Alkali Metals) you already know these soft, low-density metals as the group that reacts readily with water and air. This note explains the reactivity trend down the group using electron shells: every alkali metal atom has one outer electron to lose, and losing that electron becomes easier the further it sits from the nucleus.

modules.title: Group 1: Reactivity & Electronic Configurations
modules.opening: Every Group 1 atom carries exactly one electron in its outermost shell, and that single electron governs the metal's chemistry. When a Group 1 element reacts, its atom only needs to lose that one electron, so a 1+ ion forms at once. The shell beneath is already full, so the ion ends up with the same stable electron arrangement as a noble gas.
keyPoints: On descending Group 1, each metal reacts more vigorously than the one above it.
When a Group 1 element reacts, its atom needs to lose only the single electron in its outer shell.
Losing that outer electron forms a 1+ ion with a full outer shell.
The filled shell underneath becomes the outermost shell, so the ion gains a noble gas configuration.
Sharing the one-outer-electron pattern is why the alkali metals have such similar reactions.

low.restatement: Group 1 metals react by losing their single outer electron, which forms a 1+ ion with a full outer shell. The reactivity rises as you go down the group because that electron is lost more easily.
low.analogy: Picture peeling a sticker stuck at one corner instead of at its centre: the looser the corner, the less effort the peel takes.
low.examPointer: Questions usually ask for the trend first and then the explanation with electron shells, so give both the trend and the reason.

medium.restatement: Each Group 1 atom has one outer electron, and losing it produces a 1+ ion whose new outermost shell is already full, matching a noble gas. Reactivity increases down the group because each element adds a shell, so the outer electron sits further from the nucleus.
medium.analogy: Model the nucleus as a magnet and the outer electron as a paper clip: extra sheets of paper between them weaken the pull, so the clip detaches more readily.
medium.examPointer: Examiners expect distance and attraction in the answer: greater distance means weaker attraction, so less energy removes the electron.

modules.title: Electronic configuration of Group 1 elements
modules.opening: As you descend Group 1, each element adds one more filled shell of electrons, so the atoms grow larger step by step. The outermost electron therefore sits further and further from the positive nucleus, and the pull it feels grows weaker. Weaker attraction means less energy is needed to remove the electron, which is why the metals react more readily down the group.
keyPoints: Going down Group 1, the number of electron shells rises by one at each element.
The extra shell places the outermost electron further away from the nucleus.
Greater distance weakens the pull between the nucleus and that outermost electron.
Less energy is needed to overcome the weaker attraction, so the outer electron is lost more easily.
Lithium, sodium and potassium therefore show steadily increasing reactivity on descending the group.

low.restatement: Each step down Group 1 adds a filled shell, pushing the lone outer electron further out. The weaker pull from the nucleus means the electron is given up more easily, so reactivity climbs.
low.analogy: It is like holding a magnet further and further from a paper clip: at some distance the clip barely feels the pull and drops away at the slightest nudge.
low.examPointer: Shell diagrams of lithium, sodium and potassium are common exam artwork; link the growing shell count to easier electron loss.

medium.restatement: On descending the group each element gains a complete additional shell, increasing the distance between the nucleus and the outermost electron. The electrostatic attraction falls with distance, so a smaller energy input removes the electron and reactivity increases from lithium to potassium.
medium.analogy: Treat the attraction like gravity with distance: a satellite in a far orbit escapes with a small push, while a low orbit demands a powerful engine.
medium.examPointer: Full-mark answers chain the ideas in order: more shells, greater distance, weaker attraction, less energy, easier loss, higher reactivity.

glossary.definition: The way electrons are arranged in the shells of an atom, counted from the innermost shell outwards.
The reactive metals of Group 1, which all carry one electron in their outermost shell.
A charged particle formed when an atom loses or gains electrons.
The positively charged centre of an atom, where nearly all of its mass is concentrated.
One of the unreactive Group 0 elements, whose atoms already have complete outer shells.

workedExample.prompt: Lithium, sodium and potassium all sit in Group 1. a) State the reactivity trend down the group and explain it in terms of electronic configurations. b) Why does the ion formed always carry a 1+ charge and a noble-gas configuration?
steps: a) Reactivity increases down the group: each element adds one more filled shell, so the single outer electron sits further from the nucleus.
The greater distance weakens the attraction between the nucleus and that outer electron, so less energy is needed to remove it and the metal reacts more readily.
b) Each Group 1 atom has exactly 1 electron in its outer shell, so reacting means losing just that one electron, forming a 1+ ion.
The next shell down is already full, so the ion automatically gains a noble-gas configuration.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Reactivity rises down the group — more shells means greater distance, weaker attraction, easier electron loss. b) One outer electron lost gives 1+; the filled shell below gives the noble-gas arrangement.
